source.title: Machine learning for modular multiplication
source.authors: Kristin E. Lauter; C. Li; Krystal Maughan; Rachel Newton; Megha Srivastava

record.tranche_reason: The study trains transformers on modular multiplication and measures training and held-out test performance, providing a conceptual test of whether the claimed delayed generalization occurs in this algorithmic setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results from its own modular-multiplication experiments. It also cites grokking results from other work; those cited results are not recorded here. The test-accuracy statement is an aggregate description across different primes, bases, and secrets, rather than separately reported values for each setting.
record.test_reason: Grokking is cited only as the reason for choosing transformers. Training used early stopping once validation loss rose for 5 epochs, which cuts off the long post-overfitting phase grokking needs. No test-accuracy trajectory after training accuracy saturates is reported. The setting also differs from the originals: multi-token sequence output in base B rather than a single-token output. So the reported near-0% test accuracy cannot show whether delayed generalization occurs. The study does not test V1 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that circular regression does not consistently beat exhaustive search, and that the seq2seq transformer generalizes poorly (near-0% test accuracy). Both results are taken as evidence that modular multiplication is hard, which bears on cryptography. The authors make no claim about grokking itself.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a sequence-to-sequence transformer to predict modular multiplication outputs, and also tests circular regression on a noisy one-dimensional LWE task. It does not reproduce the original grokking setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that base representation affects memorization; beam search generally outperforms greedy decoding, increasing beam size beyond 3 makes no difference, sinusoidal positional encoding improves over random encoding only for smaller moduli, and weighted loss generally improves generalization. Increasing transformer layers helps only for smaller moduli.

fits_no_version.finding: Sequence-to-sequence transformers trained with early stopping on modular multiplication (p from 83 to 293, bases 7–11) can memorize training data for small p. Exact held-out accuracy is largely 0%, while arithmetic difference and test loss decrease during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformers emitting multi-token base-B outputs fail to generalize on modular multiplication within early-stopped training budgets.

record.problems: The test-accuracy result is described broadly as 'largely 0%' without per-setting values or uncertainty. The study does not report a training-set-size sweep or a test-accuracy trajectory establishing whether delayed generalization occurs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. The paper's arithmetic-difference trend in Figure 3.1 is not an accuracy result and does not measure the circuit or mechanism named in V2.

untested.parts: All of it. Test accuracy over long training after train saturation is never tracked, early stopping truncates training, and training-set size is not varied.
All of it. No circuits or progress measures are studied.
All of it. No weight decay or norm manipulation, and no critical dataset size.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges V1' label is unsupported. Early stopping on rising validation loss, together with the absence of any post-saturation test curve, means the study could not have observed grokking. The setting (multi-token outputs, the KL loss used, no reported weight decay) also departs from the original recipe. Grokking appears only as cited motivation (refs 4, 9, 11).

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary training-set size to test whether smaller training sets require more optimization, and does not report a training trajectory showing whether test accuracy rises long after training accuracy saturates.
The study does not identify or track a generalizing circuit, memorizing components, or mechanistic progress measures.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep is tested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
The study does not test weight decay or a low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
The study does not identify and compare algorithms learned across runs.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations for grokking.

rows.value: largely 0% across different choices of prime modulus, base, and secret
rows.note: The paper reports a broad aggregate characterization, not per-setting test-accuracy values. It does not give a chance-level reference.
rows.check: Test accuracy comes from models trained with validation-loss early stopping, which precludes the long-training regime grokking describes. An aggregate 'largely 0%' cannot show whether a late jump would occur. It should not be read as challenging V1.
